ambiguities.question: On a CJK-exempt side, does a zero-width joiner or non-joiner immediately next to the match block it (it is a word character but neither a base character nor a combining mark), or is it ignored like neighbouring base characters?

citations.excerpt: the boundary check ignores neighbouring base characters, because those scripts are written without spaces; a combining mark immediately next to the match still blocks it on that side

findings.description: The CJK side rule protects only combining marks (Mn, Mc, Me). Other characters that extend the previous character are not covered: the halfwidth katakana voiced and semi-voiced sound marks U+FF9E/U+FF9F are Lm (Other_Grapheme_Extend), and conjoining hangul jamo in NFD (vowel and trailing consonant jamo, Lo) continue a syllable. A rule ending in a kana or hangul character can therefore match the base of a halfwidth voiced kana or the leading jamo of a decomposed syllable and leave the extender orphaned. Normal ASR output (NFC, fullwidth) does not trigger it.
findings.suggestion: Either state that a match never starts or ends inside an extended grapheme cluster (UAX #29) on a CJK side, which covers marks, the halfwidth sound marks and jamo, or document these two cases as accepted limitations in Edge Cases.

citations.excerpt: a combining mark immediately next to the match still blocks it on that side
CJK side next to a combining mark: the CJK exemption ignores neighbouring base characters only.

findings.description: The exempted script list does not follow its own rationale: hangul is exempted although Korean is written with spaces, while Thai, Lao, Khmer and Myanmar, written without spaces, are not exempted, so rules are almost inert in unspaced text in those scripts. The behavior is safe (no corruption) but its rationale is wrong for Korean and silent for the other scripts.
findings.suggestion: Name the exempted scripts with a per-script rationale (for Korean: particles attach to the noun) and document that rules match only space-delimited words in Thai, Lao, Khmer and Myanmar.

citations.excerpt: On a side where the recognized text begins or ends with a CJK ideograph, kana or hangul character, the boundary check ignores neighbouring base characters, because those scripts are written without spaces

findings.description: A combining mark before a CJK-side match belongs to the preceding character, not to the match, yet it blocks the match. The same text therefore behaves differently in NFC and NFD: the rule かい replaces inside ぎかい written in NFC but not in NFD. This is a false negative, never a corruption.
findings.suggestion: Accept and document, or limit the mark rule to the side where the mark would be orphaned (after the match).

citations.excerpt: a combining mark immediately next to the match still blocks it on that side

findings.description: Recognizing the header by its trimmed fields widens the header to spaced forms such as `recognized ; replacement`. A hand-written file without a header whose first content line is the genuine rule recognized to replacement loses that rule; the preview reports the line as ignored, and exported or bulk-edited text always starts with the canonical header, so round-trips are unaffected.
findings.suggestion: Acceptable; optionally mention in Edge Cases that a first content line equal to a header pair is always a header.

citations.excerpt: The first line that is neither blank nor a comment is ignored as a header when its two fields, split like a rule line and trimmed

findings.description: The length unit (Unicode scalar or grapheme) is not stated, and the normalized key applies no canonical normalization, so café in NFC and NFD are two distinct keys that display alike.
findings.suggestion: State 'Unicode scalar values, no canonical normalization', or normalize keys to NFC.

citations.excerpt: the trimmed recognized text has 1–100 characters
